claims.text: The starting material is a near-equiatomic Ni-Co-Cu-Fe solid-solution nanoparticle system containing minimal Pt.
The starting nanoparticles have a uniform elemental distribution.
Short-duration oxidation at low oxygen partial pressure and 773–1173 K will form a surface oxide layer.
The oxidation treatment will produce an ultrathin and uniform oxide layer.
The oxide layer acts as a physical barrier that limits surface diffusion.
Atomic migration during high-temperature exposure can cause elemental segregation.
Atomic migration during high-temperature exposure can cause nanoparticle coarsening.
Suppressing surface diffusion will inhibit elemental segregation.
Suppressing surface diffusion will inhibit particle coarsening.
Oxidized nanoparticles will retain a near-equiatomic composition during high-temperature service better than unoxidized nanoparticles.
Oxidized nanoparticles will retain well-defined particle sizes during high-temperature service better than unoxidized nanoparticles.
Untreated nanoparticles will exhibit greater elemental segregation during high-temperature service.
Untreated nanoparticles will exhibit greater sintering during high-temperature service.
Improved structural and chemical uniformity will preserve catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
The proposed stabilization mechanism is effective over 773–1173 K for catalytic operation if the oxide remains ultrathin.
The same oxide-mediated stabilization mechanism applies under analogous thermoelectric operating conditions.
Excessive oxidation caused by high oxygen partial pressure or prolonged exposure may compromise catalytic activity.
